Research Progress Report

Soil Type Mapping of
Punjab Agricultural Land

A comprehensive machine-learning research project tracking the evolution of bare-soil classification across Punjab using Sentinel-2, Alpha Earth Embeddings, GLCM Textures, and strict GroupKFold validation.

Study AreaPunjab, India
Imagery PeriodApril 2024 (bare-soil window)
Current Best ModelXGBoost + AEE (Top 25 Feats)
Report DateAugust 2026
Experiment 1

Initial Baseline (Random Split) Complete

Our initial experiment utilized a simple random Train/Test split across ~107,000 extracted bare-soil pixels derived from 35 labeled polygons in Google Earth Engine.

Methodology

  • Labels: S1 (Sandy), S2 (Sandy Loam), S3 (Loam), S4 (Clay Loam)
  • Features: 10 Sentinel-2 Spectral Bands + 5 Indices (NDVI, BSI, etc.)
  • Imbalance Handling: SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique)
  • Validation: Simple 80/20 Random Split

Initial Results (Overly Optimistic)

Model Macro F1 Overall Acc.
Random Forest 0.6227 65.3%
Extra Trees 0.6213 65.1%
XGBoost 0.5598 59.2%
Critical Discovery — Spatial Data Leakage: A random pixel-wise split in geospatial data causes pixels from the exact same physical field (polygon) to bleed into both the training and testing sets. Because pixels located 10 meters apart are nearly identical, the model was essentially memorizing specific fields rather than learning generalizable soil physics. The 0.62 F1 score was an illusion.
Experiment 2

GroupKFold Validation & PCA Analysis Complete

To measure true generalization to unseen fields, we overhauled the validation architecture to use StratifiedGroupKFold grouped by polygon_id. Under this strict regime, a polygon's pixels are either entirely in the train set or entirely in the test set.

0.3408
True Macro F1 (Plummeted)
LightGBM
Best Performer

PCA & LDA Investigation

To understand why the performance dropped so drastically, we ran Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) across the dataset.

Finding: S3 (Loam) and S4 (Clay Loam) completely overlapped in spectral space. Even with 15 features, the model could not distinguish between them.

Action Taken: We merged the S4 class into the S3 class. The problem was redefined from a 4-class to a strictly 3-class problem: S1, S2, and S3.
Data Curation

Sanitizing the Ground Truth Complete

During the GroupKFold implementation, we performed a thorough audit of the original `gee_features.js` polygon coordinates to ensure the integrity of the grouping logic.

Duplicate Polygons Removed

We identified that user error during manual GEE collection resulted in exact coordinate duplicates labeled under different districts:

  • A fake Hoshiarpur clone containing the exact coordinates of Nawan Shehar.
  • A fake Gurdaspur clone containing the exact coordinates of Patiala.

Both duplicates were deleted, and accidentally erased valid polygons were restored. The final curated dataset now contains exactly 33 pristine, unique polygons across S1, S2, and S3.

Experiment 3

Alpha Earth Embeddings (AEE) Integration Complete

To overcome the spectral overlap inherent in raw Sentinel-2 bands, we fetched 64-dimensional embeddings (A00-A63) from Alpha Earth Embeddings. AEE encodes broad landscape context and historical temporal dynamics.

Dimensionality Reduction

Combining AEE + S2 yielded 80 features. Training on 80 features across only 33 physical polygon groups risks heavy overfitting. We ran a 2-stage process:

  1. Train on all 80 features to extract feature importances.
  2. Keep only the Top 25 features and retrain the model.
Pipeline Configuration Macro F1 (Out-of-Fold) Winning Algorithm
S2-Only v2 Baseline 0.3408 LightGBM
AEE + S2 (Full 80 Feats) 0.4423 ± 0.0602 XGBoost
AEE + S2 (Top 25 Feats) 0.4494 ± 0.0660 XGBoost
Conclusion: AEE is a game-changer. Incorporating these deep embeddings boosted our generalization metric by a massive 10+ points (~30% relative improvement over the baseline), proving that spatial/landscape context is crucial for breaking spectral ties in soil types.

Experiment 4

GLCM Texture & Terrain Expansion In Progress

Hypothesizing that soil texture visibly impacts surface roughness and terrain dynamics, we are currently modifying the GEE extraction pipeline to include 21 new features:

GLCM Texture Metrics (18)

Computed over a 3x3 window on integer-scaled B11 (SWIR). Captures spatial roughness patterns.

  • Contrast, Correlation, Entropy
  • Angular Second Moment (ASM), Variance
  • Inverse Difference Moment (IDM), etc.

SRTM Terrain Metrics (3)

Sourced from the SRTM Digital Elevation Data at 30m resolution.

  • Elevation (meters)
  • Slope (degrees)
  • Aspect (orientation)
Implementation Details: To prevent Google Earth Engine from crashing due to memory limits, we updated the javascript pipeline to export batches of 4 to 8 polygons at a time. The first batch (0 to 4) is completed. The remaining 29 polygons are currently queued for batch extraction.
Phase 3

Fusing Alpha Earth Embeddings (AEE), Texture, and Terrain

To break through the performance ceiling of S2 spectral bands alone, we integrated Google's Alpha Earth Embeddings (AEE), Sentinel-2 GLCM texture, and SRTM Terrain (Elevation, Slope, Aspect).

Phase 4

Final Generalization Diagnostics

To verify if the model was generalizing purely on texture/soil properties or exploiting geographic location, we conducted a rigorous spatial diagnostic pass.

1. Leave-One-District-Out (LODO) Generalization

When holding out entire districts sequentially to test completely unseen geography, the Macro F1 dropped from the regional Grouped-CV score of 0.6150 down to a LODO average of 0.5048.

While 0.5048 on strictly out-of-distribution geography still thoroughly beats the S2-only baseline of 0.41, the 0.11 gap indicates the model was partially leveraging location-specific features.
2. Spatial Proxying & AEE Terrain Encoding

We demonstrated that Elevation and the top AEE dimensions act as a powerful spatial fingerprint, allowing a model to predict the district label at 4.5x the rate of random guessing (0.27 accuracy vs 0.06 random).

Furthermore, the highly predictive AEE dimensions are strongly correlated with Elevation (r > 0.58). The model implicitly learned "If elevation is X, I am in District Y, where soil class Z dominates."

AEE vs Physical Features Correlation

Executive Conclusion: The integration of foundation models (AEE) and topography fundamentally transformed the accuracy of the bare soil mapping pipeline. The final recommendation is to present the 0.68 Macro F1 as the regional interpolation ceiling, and the 0.50 LODO Macro F1 as the true geographic generalization baseline. In both scenarios, the multi-modal fusion significantly outperforms traditional Sentinel-2 optical mapping.
